history.origins: Traversone (also Ciapanò, Rovescino) is the reverse game of Tressette. The name Ciapanò is Milanese dialect for "Don't catch it!". It was very popular in Lombardy until the 1980s and is still played there; in Central Italy it is known as Traversone. The goal is to avoid taking point cards—whoever reaches the agreed penalty total (often 21 or 31) loses. Play is anticlockwise like most Italian card games.
timeline: 20th century: Popular in Lombardy; reverse variant of Tressette documented.
history.evolution: Popular alternative to standard Tressette across Italy.

rules.objective: Avoid taking tricks with point cards. Player reaching 21 penalty points LOSES.
rules.gameplay: Same as Tressette play: Must follow suit. No trumps. Highest of led suit wins. But scoring is inverted â€” points are BAD.

strategy.basic: Avoid Aces (they're worth the most penalty). Dump high cards on others' leads.
strategy.intermediate: Deliberately go for Cappotto if you have overwhelming strength (reverses penalty to opponents).
strategy.advanced: Count points taken. Decide when to attempt Cappotto vs play safe.
tips: The last trick is worth 1 penalty point.
Cappotto is a high-risk, high-reward move.
